details:
Aurora Base is a browser-based survival management game set on a Mars research outpost. The player commands a crew of four astronauts across five Martian sols, deciding how to allocate limited energy, oxygen, food and science while the environment throws escalating crises at them. Each sol presents an event — a dust storm, a solar flare, a greenhouse failure, a delayed communication window — and the player chooses among two or more responses. Every choice has an immediate effect and a delayed consequence that surfaces two or three sols later. The game ends with a mission report that traces the outcome back to the decisions that caused it, so the player learns that survival on Mars is a chain of trade-offs, not a single lucky call.

How it works. Events are stored in a data file separate from the game logic, so the simulation engine applies rules while content stays editable. Resources deplete at night and regenerate during the day. Between sols, the player spends collected parts on upgrades — larger battery, extended suit oxygen, faster boots — which is what makes each run different from the last. Outside the base, a small exploration map lets the player leave on foot to gather ice, rock samples or salvage from a crashed capsule. The suit's oxygen is the hard limit: the further you go, the more you bring back, but you must return before the tank empties.

Benefits and intended impact. Most space-education content for children is passive — a video, an article, a quiz. Aurora Base turns the constraints of Mars habitation into something a player feels directly: you cannot have heat, food and air at the same time without planning. The design targets ages 7 to 12, with a Cadet mode that pauses the clock while an event is open and highlights the most urgent action, so younger players are not blocked by reading speed. The intended impact is to make the engineering trade-offs of a Mars mission intuitive before a student ever encounters them in a textbook.

Tools and technologies. The project was initially prototyped in Godot Engine and migrated to a web stack — HTML, CSS and JavaScript — to guarantee a playable link within the hackathon window. Event and upgrade definitions live in JSON data files, keeping content separate from the simulation logic. Pixel art assets were created and recolored in-house, with a 32×32 character sprite and four-frame run cycle. The game runs in any modern browser with no installation and supports keyboard, mouse and on-screen touch controls for mobile.

Creativity and considerations. The creative core is consequence visibility: instead of hiding the effects of a choice, the final report explicitly links each decision to its later outcome, turning a game over into a lesson. The team prioritized scope discipline over polish — shipping five complete sols and a real ending before adding languages or visual detail — and treated browser compatibility as the top technical risk, testing it early rather than at the deadline.
